Deliverable 7.1.1: Report on marine growth modeling methods and Deliverable 7.2.1: Report on marine growth impact on RM3 performance The report for Deliverable 7.1.1 and 7.2.1 as originally submitted is appended. Additional analysis can be found in the ACC papers, which are also appended. (The PI regards the contents of the ACC papers – Deliverable 7.4.2 -- to be the best final summary of the overall project effort.) In summary, the literature review establishes that biofouling is problematic for marine energy because high plankton levels—a biofouling indicator—correlate geographically with areas of greatest wave energy density. Prior studies have found varying impacts: experimental work on the Oyster800 showed up to 15% power reduction depending on kelp growth location, simulations of a Waves4Power buoy predicted up to 25% power loss over 25 years with 40% occurring in the first year, while a Lysekil buoy study found no power impact due to its high damping and mass ratio. The report also summarizes research on how biofouling affects drag coefficients and adds mass (ranging from 5–40 kg/m² depending on species). The simulation study uses WEC-Sim to model biofouling effects on the RM3 reference model, developing a drag coefficient model based on surface roughness for axially-oriented cylinders. Results show that increasing roughness from 1 mm to 1 m reduces average PTO power by approximately 7% under regular seas (T=10 s) and by 11–22% under irregular seas with a Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum, with the system being most sensitive to initial small perturbations in roughness. These findings have 4 important implications for WEC controller design, as both surface roughness and added mass must be accounted for to maintain optimal power extraction over the device's operational lifetime. Deliverable 7.3.1: Report on list of components, modes, and threats most likely to result in a WEC fault or failure The report for Deliverable 7.3.1 as originally submitted is appended. In summary, the fault reconnaissance study systematically evaluated failure mechanisms across six major WEC subsystems: generator, power electronic switches, WEC body, mooring lines, O-rings/seals, and PTO. Each failure mode was ranked on a 1-5 scale for both probability and severity, with severity quantified in dollars per year based on work time, crew requirements, vessel costs, and lost revenue for a 100 kW reference WEC. Biofouling on the WEC body emerged as a high-risk item at approximately $204,000/year, driven by inevitable marine growth reaching 100% coverage within 500 days and causing up to 45% power reduction. PTO failures are a roughly $254,000/year risk due to system complexity requiring extensive repair time and potential drydocking. The analysis also identified corrosion as a prevalent failure mechanism across multiple components, with O-ring and seal corrosion presenting approximately $96,000/year in risk due to accelerated degradation in saltwater environments. Extreme sea states posed $169,000/year risk to mooring systems.
